physical_harm: Killed husband of PW2 by strangulation and assaulted PW2, PW5, PW6, and PW1 with iron rods
number_of_offences: Three counts charged under Sections 395, 396, and 397 IPC; conviction for Sections 395 and 397 upheld, conviction for Section 396 overturned
key_evidence_accepted: The recovery of the weapon stated to be at the instance of A2 cannot be connected to the crime
witness_credibility: PW1 and PW2 could not have identified A2 in the court at that distance of time. They were guided by the photographs repeatedly shown by the police. Evidently, the witnesses did not know the accused earlier, hence the accused could be identified only through a test identification parade which was not done in this case, so far as A-2 is concerned.
post_offence_conduct: A2 was arrested after a period of ten years, in connection with some other case

legal_representation.accused: Sanjay Jain, Sudhakar Kulwant, Rachna Golcha, Afshan Pracha
legal_representation.state: C. Paramasivam, M. Yogesh Kanna (for B. Balaji)

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
procedural_irregularity: No identification parade conducted for A2, witnesses could not properly identify him in court

appeal_history.high_court: Conviction confirmed, sentence modified to life imprisonment
appeal_history.supreme_court: Appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellants and nine other absconding accused entered the house of PW 2, armed with iron rods, with the intention of committing burglary. They killed the husband of PW 2 by strangulating him with a rope and assaulted PW 2, PW 5, PW 6, and PW 1 with iron rods. The iron rod used 10 years back was recovered at the instance of A2.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of A2 beyond reasonable doubt. There was no identification parade for A2, and the witnesses could not properly identify him. The recovered weapon could not be connected to the crime, and the prosecution could not establish a nexus between the recovered rod and the crime alleged.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that clear reasoning and analysis are essential in judicial decisions. The court emphasized that the death sentence must be awarded only in the 'rarest of rare cases' and that the trial court's decision must be based on settled judicial precedents and not influenced by personal opinions or speeches.
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh and Ors. v. State of Punjab (1983) 3 SCC 470; Ravindra Alias Ravi Bansi Gohar v. State of Maharashtra and Ors. (1998) 6 SCC 609; Dwarkadas Gehanmal v. State of Gujarat (1999) 1 SCC 57; Mustkeem alias Sirajudeen v. State of Rajasthan (2011) 11 SCC 724; William Henry Furman v. State of Georgia 408 U.S. 238 (1972); Gregg v. Georgia 428 U.S. 153 (1976); C. Muniappan v. State of T.N. (2010) 9 SCC 567; Dara Singh v. Republic of India (2011) 2 SCC 490; Surendra Kofi v. State of U.P. (2011) 4 SCC 80; Mohd. Mannan v. State of Bihar (2011) 5 SCC 509; Sudam v. State of Maharashtra (2011) 7 SCC 125; Sham Alias Kishore Bhaskarrao Matkari v. State of Maharashtra (2011) 10 SCC 389; Mohammed Ajmal Mohammad Amir Kasab alias Abu Mujahid v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 9 SCC 1
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was not imposed as the Supreme Court held that the trial court's manner of awarding the death sentence was in complete disregard of the tests laid down by the Supreme Court for determining the 'rarest of rare cases'. The court found the trial judge's reasoning to be flawed and not based on proper legal principles or precedents.
